title: Built on a Weekend: Damien Riehl and Mike Bommarito Show What Vibe Coding Can Really Do
author: Damien Riehl · Mike Bommarito

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The excerpt is only a general invitation to follow Folio’s future activity. It provides no substantive claims about cautious experimentation, collaboration, trust, customer outcomes, distributed expertise or demonstrated transformation, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.
qs: So really, we're stay tuned for what Folio is going to be doing.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core idea that structured expertise and requirements can become product infrastructure, and adds a concrete implementation mechanism: AI-assisted coding can translate product requirements rapidly into legal-tech demonstrations such as document-tagging interfaces. Its contribution is limited to practitioner claims and demonstrations, without evidence of reliable production workflows, evaluation, or commercial transformation.
qs: But right now the product requirement document is the code.
So now you can very easily see on this website why it is valuable to have these tags.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s value depends on redesigning legal work around human expertise, structured knowledge and controlled implementation. It materially extends the synthesis by proposing interoperable matter data and AI-assisted tool-building by legal subject-matter experts as concrete mechanisms for workflow redesign and improved pricing, while acknowledging security, privilege and court-data constraints. Its evidence is chiefly demonstration-based and predictive rather than proof of broad organisational value.
qs: This interoperability of data, the ability to map from historical unstructured information to structured and critically structured and interoperable information is what is going to allow us to build pricing models, whether it's within a firm across years or decades of  different practice area or across multiple firms or across multiple corporates who all have data that can be aggregated or across both sides.
That is a subject matter expert plus a developer maybe can move faster and maybe around the edges make it more secure or something like that.

kp.k: AI coding compresses legal technology development timelines
kp.d: Riehl contrasts previously writing extensive product requirements for developers with using Claude Code to implement those requirements himself. He reports building Folio tools during the preceding month, including Enrich over a weekend, using a $200 monthly subscription. These are accounts of his own development experience, rather than measured comparisons across development teams. His claim that this was impossible in November 2025 is qualified in the discussion as referring to building so quickly.
qs: I would spend, know, I create a hundred pages saying the document, the product needs to be doing these 100 pages worth of things. And then it would take the coders a year to do it.
It took me literally, like I've done all of these things in the last month.
And with zero dollars, or I take that back, with $200 a month in the top cloud code subscription.

kp.k: Open legal standards enable interoperability across market participants
kp.d: Riehl describes SALI as a shared legal data standard connecting corporations, firms and software vendors. He reports expanding its vocabulary from a thousand to 18,000 tags and forking its MIT-licensed ontology in 2024 to create Folio with Bommarito. Folio extends the vocabulary and adds implementation tools; unique concept identifiers are intended to connect different labels and taxonomies across systems.
qs: we built it from a thousand tags to 18,000 tags.

Those are all SALI tags that if you want to be able to push and pull data from Microsoft to their law firm, to their legal technology vendor, all of them can speak the same language to make that data interoperable.
So we did a fork under the MIT license to create what is now Folio.

kp.k: Accessible interfaces reduce barriers to implementing legal ontologies
kp.d: Riehl presents Folio Explorer as a response to the login and browsing friction of WebProtege, enabling users to inspect concepts, definitions and identifiers without an account. Folio Mapper addresses a separate implementation problem: converting existing firm taxonomies into multiple, more granular Folio concepts. The demonstration includes user selection of proposed mappings and exports for review or reuse, rather than an assertion that every mapping should be accepted automatically.
qs: This is just an open website where I can be able to browse all the areas of law.
I want to find all the enforcements, which are different than the investigations.
I can upload my Excel spreadsheet or my CSV file or my text file.
I could send it as an Excel spreadsheet or as a CSV file. Or as a Markdown file.

kp.k: Document enrichment combines symbolic matching and language models
kp.d: Riehl demonstrates Folio Enrich tagging time entries and legal work product through a reported 16-stage process. Literal ontology matching and LLM extraction operate in parallel, followed by reconciliation, nested-span handling, confidence ranking and contextual assessment by an LLM judge. He shows confidence scores of 85% and 95% based on agreement among sources; these are tool-generated scores, not reported benchmark accuracy results or human verification.
qs: Stage one is ingesting the text, normalizing the text.
And then parallel, the large language model pulls out motion to dismiss from it.
So here you can see the confidence score is 85%. And the confidence score for complaint is 95%.
And then we have a judge, a large language model judge say, now analyze this in the context of the entire sentence or in the context of the entire paragraph.
So now it's gone through a 16 stage pass.

kp.k: Knowledge graphs support structured retrieval and reliability claims
kp.d: Riehl argues that extracting noun–verb–noun relationships enables searches for factual patterns, such as officers using tasers, alongside legal concepts. He characterizes the combination of neural models and symbolic knowledge graphs as more deterministic and reliable. His statements that symbolic triples are accurate 100% of the time and LLMs might be accurate 50% or 80% of the time are assertions in the demonstration, not findings attributed to a study.
qs: So you could be able to say, hey, show me all of the cases where a taser was used by an officer.
This is a knowledge graph. To be able to say noun, verb, noun, and this will 100 % of the time be accurate.
But a large language model, might 50 % of the time be accurate or 80 % of the time be accurate.

So this neural symbolic combination to have neural net AI, large language models, combined with good old fashioned AI, knowledge graphs, will give you much more deterministic, therefore reliable things.

kp.k: Structured historical data underpins alternative pricing models
kp.d: Bommarito argues that moving beyond hourly billing requires pricing models grounded in structured, consistent and interoperable historical information. He envisages using data within firms, across firms and corporate legal departments, or across both provider and buyer sides. Riehl adds that Folio captures the contextual variables lawyers invoke when saying pricing depends on circumstances. This is a proposed enabling mechanism, not evidence that the demonstrated tools have already produced a transition away from hourly billing.
qs: Because in the absence of a pricing model, well, we know what the alternative is. It's the status quo.

This interoperability of data, the ability to map from historical unstructured information to structured and critically structured and interoperable information is what is going to allow us to build pricing models
this is how we get to the future of a post-billable model, or at least some things being post-billable hour.
So really this is counting all of the it depends that will really push the pricing up or down.

kp.k: MCP connects ontology tools to agentic legal workflows
kp.d: Bommarito demonstrates Claude Code fetching a complaint from CourtListener and using Folio tools and skills to classify litigation objectives with standardized identifiers. He estimates that the displayed classification takes 30 to 60 seconds and proposes extending the approach to document-management systems and corporate matter histories. His further estimate that a hundred thousand documents could be enriched overnight for a couple hundred dollars in tokens is a scale-and-cost claim, not a reported corpus evaluation.
qs: we built everything or much of what you saw there on the screen into MCP tools or resources that any MCP compatible system can utilize.
In this case, We've given it, like I said, a number of MCP tools, resources related to folio, and then a number of skills.
it is spitting out here all of the objectives including the folio standards and IDs with descriptions.
It's like for a couple hundred dollars in tokens, you can go through a hundred thousand documents in a DMS. overnight while you're sleeping and have rich interoperable data.

kp.k: Collaborative ontology editing abstracts away technical governance
kp.d: Riehl describes OntoKit as replacing inefficient email-based ontology revision with an interface that records edits in GitHub branches without requiring users to operate GitHub directly. After 30 minutes without further edits, the system creates a pull request for suggested changes. Developed in collaboration with a priest working on Catholic ontologies, the tool is presented as a reusable mechanism for crowdsourcing Folio and other ontologies.
qs: it's actually created a branch in GitHub.
You don't even know it.
you stop making these edits for, 30 minutes, that creates what's called a pull request.
So this is a way you can crowdsource an ontology.

kp.k: Open Gloss extends structured representation beyond legal concepts
kp.d: The speakers present Open Gloss as a complementary vocabulary of 150,000 concepts covering factual subject matter, definitions, word senses and relationships, linked through unique identifiers. Bommarito reports creating it in a weekend for under $1,000 in tokens. Riehl proposes combining these concepts with Folio's legal ontology to retrieve matters by facts and law. The examples concern conceptual representation, rather than verification of the truth of clients' factual accounts.
qs: he did 150,000 of these things, all with this beautiful, unique identifier.
It was a weekend and under a grand in tokens.
And now you have the facts plus the law in folio.
You can download it in GitHub or you can go to Hugging Face and be able to take the 1. 28 gigabyte file that is the output and run it locally on your own machine

kp.k: Open-source reuse and local deployment widen implementation options
kp.d: Riehl argues that firms need not reproduce the creators' expertise from scratch because they can direct coding tools to customize the open-source repositories. He describes using different cloud model providers or local models, including disconnected operation. Bommarito connects controlled deployment environments to privilege requirements and highlights security boundaries in his demonstration; these remarks describe deployment choices rather than establishing compliance for every use.
qs: Because you can go to Fully Unrich and literally point cloud code to this URL, saying take this URL and then customize it to the thing I care about.
I could use Gemini or I could use open AI Anthropic or I could use one of the local models
unplug from the internet and do this work locally
in a controlled environment that satisfies privilege requirements, for example.

kp.k: Subject expertise may become more important than developer headcount
kp.d: Riehl predicts that AI coding will give subject-matter experts greater control over product development across firms, in-house legal departments and vendors. He argues that requirements and legal knowledge become more decisive as implementation accelerates, while acknowledging that developers may improve speed and security. Bommarito qualifies the broader enthusiasm through a tool-use analogy: easier tools still require knowing when and how to use them.
qs: maybe the people that are gonna win this game are not the people that have the most developers, but the people that have the most subject matter expertise.
And so I would say that's true for law firms. It's true for in-house law departments. Also true for legal tech companies.
a subject matter expert plus a developer maybe can move faster and maybe around the edges make it more secure or something like that.
there is still a threshold in terms of knowing when and how to use the tool, no matter how easy the tool is compared to what came before.

kp.k: Firms should develop internal product-building capabilities
kp.d: Bommarito recommends identifying, supporting or hiring people who combine legal knowledge with tool-building capability, predicting a changed human-capital mix and greater internal product development. Speaking from his commercial work with smaller firms and boutiques, he argues that focused practices can now build previously unavailable tools using inexpensive subscriptions. The speakers also anticipate pressure on consultancy prices and favor teaching clients to use the tools, rather than simply delivering finished systems.
qs: Every law firm needs at least one Damien.
the human capital mix at firms is going to change.
The sooner you get a person, who can start a flywheel of productization and internal product development, the better you will be situated in particular as a firm to navigate this transition.
I actually think now is a great time to be a small and medium sized firm with focus
Certainly the cost that the market will bear will change.

kp.k: Court-data access remains a constraint despite cheaper development
kp.d: Bommarito identifies PACER and state-court access restrictions as continuing limits on legal technology and research, even when processing tools become easier to build. His qualification is that obtaining current precedent can remain difficult or impossible where courts do not make it readily accessible. Riehl also identifies legal research applications for enrichment, but his reference to forthcoming Clio work is prospective rather than a demonstrated research product.
qs: there's still pacer, there's still state court gates.
Unless and until those gates are removed, there will continue to be ceilings on what is possible.
if I need precedent up to date from courts that are not easily accessed or publicly available, what do I do?
So really, this has huge implications for legal research.

kp.k: AI collaboration complicates identifying human authorship
kp.d: In discussing AI-assisted writing, Bommarito characterizes the resulting material as joint work between humans and models and says he can no longer clearly separate their contributions. Riehl draws an analogy to machine-assisted music creation and questions the practicality of specifying human-created portions to the Copyright Office. These are the speakers' observations about attribution difficulties, not an established legal conclusion about copyright ownership.
qs: these are joint works to be honest between a tool or multiple models and us as humans
I can't honestly tell you where my contribution ended and the other side began anymore.
I'm supposed to tell the Copyright Office what parts were human created. Good luck with that.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Riehl claims AI coding lets legal subject-matter experts build substantive legal technology rapidly and cheaply, shifting competitive advantage away from developer headcount.
pts.d: Riehl presents Folio Enrich, Mapper and OntoKit as examples of tools he could build directly from requirements rather than handing specifications to developers. He predicts that legal expertise and ideas will become more important to success than having many developers, across law firms, corporate legal departments and legal-tech companies. His broad statement that developers are no longer needed is qualified by his acknowledgment that a developer can improve speed and security.

pts.k: Riehl and Bommarito claim AI combined with legal ontologies makes document enrichment, taxonomy mapping and knowledge retrieval readily implementable at scale.
pts.d: Riehl describes extracting legal concepts, entities, verbs and relationships from time entries, contracts, litigation documents and regulatory materials, then assigning standardized identifiers. Mapper translates firms' existing taxonomies into interoperable categories. Bommarito demonstrates an agent using Folio MCP tools to identify litigation objectives from a complaint and claims this makes previously aspirational knowledge-management searches straightforward. He also claims a firm could enrich 100,000 documents overnight for a few hundred dollars in tokens.

pts.k: Riehl claims combining language models with knowledge graphs produces more deterministic and reliable legal-data outputs.
pts.d: He describes Enrich's parallel literal matching and language-model extraction, reconciliation, confidence scoring and contextual review by an LLM judge. He contrasts symbolic triples with variable LLM accuracy and claims their combination improves reliability. The claim that symbolic relationships will be accurate 100% of the time is his assertion, not a reported benchmark. The LLM judge is automated output assessment, not human verification.

pts.k: Bommarito predicts that AI-enabled structuring of historical legal data will support pricing models and a partial move beyond hourly billing.
pts.d: Bommarito links standardized matter and work-product data to pricing models within firms, across firms and across corporate buyers. Riehl adds that encoding the factors behind lawyers' 'it depends' answers can identify what raises or lowers matter costs. The claim concerns enabling alternative pricing, not evidence that these tools have already caused a billing-model transition.

pts.k: Riehl claims linking legal concepts with an AI-generated general-concept resource enables fact-sensitive legal retrieval and has major legal-research implications.
pts.d: Riehl presents Open Gloss as approximately 150,000 concepts with definitions, senses, synonyms and relationships that can be linked to Folio's legal ontology. His example is finding murders involving knives by combining legal and factual identifiers. These are generalized concepts for tagging documents, not an independently established collection of client facts. Bommarito reports generating the resource over a weekend for under $1,000 in tokens. Riehl says the same enrichment approach applies to court opinions and other research materials, while leaving forthcoming commercial applications unspecified.

pts.k: Bommarito predicts changes in firms' skills mix and internal product development; both speakers anticipate pressure on consulting prices.
pts.d: Bommarito argues firms should recruit, develop or empower someone who combines legal knowledge and AI-enabled product-building ability. He claims focused small and medium-sized firms, including boutiques, can now build previously inaccessible tools without revealing proprietary processes to an outside supplier. Riehl suggests consulting should increasingly teach users to build rather than simply supply solutions, and Bommarito expects the prices the market supports to change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is first-party tool demonstrations, reported development experience and commercial experience, rather than independent performance or market studies.
pts.d: Riehl walks through the tools' interfaces, outputs, repositories and Enrich's 16-stage processing design. Mapper visibly allows users to accept or alter proposed mappings. Bommarito demonstrates objective extraction from a CourtListener complaint using Claude Code and MCP tools, estimating 30–60 seconds. Development time, subscription cost, Open Gloss generation cost and overnight document-processing economics are speaker reports; the transcript does not supply an independent audit, controlled accuracy evaluation, full cost accounting or observed pricing-transition results. Bommarito supports the small-firm opportunity claim with his work with small and medium-sized firms and boutiques. Riehl's development forecast also draws on approximately 15 years of litigation experience and prior product-development work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The speakers describe a capability shift already occurring in early 2026, with further change anticipated over the following year but no dated forecast for market-wide adoption.
pts.d: Riehl says he began using Claude Code about two months earlier and built the displayed tools within the last month, sometimes in a weekend, using a $200 monthly subscription. He explicitly clarifies that the claimed impossibility in November 2025 concerned building as quickly, not building at all. The short development period follows years of ontology development since 2020 and used Bommarito's technical setup assistance. The claims depend on usable specifications, domain knowledge and knowing how to use the tools; reuse of their open-source repositories is offered as a way to lower that threshold. The subscription figure is not presented as a comprehensive accounting of hardware, expertise or prior ontology-building costs.

pts.k: Open-source reuse, compatible integrations, secure deployment and access to underlying legal data condition the promised benefits.
pts.d: The speakers say users can customize their open-source tools through AI coding and access much of the functionality through MCP-compatible systems. They describe hosted-model and local-model options, including disconnected operation, and Bommarito shows security boundaries in his agent environment. Local or controlled deployment is offered as relevant to privilege requirements, not established as a universal compliance guarantee. Bommarito identifies PACER and state-court access barriers as continuing ceilings on legal-research capabilities, regardless of improvements in processing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span provider-side product development, firms' knowledge management and staffing, and corporate buyers' data and pricing capabilities.
pts.d: For law firms, the speakers envisage faster internal tool creation, searchable historical work, interoperable taxonomies and a greater need for legal/product-building expertise. Focused boutiques and small or medium-sized firms are presented as beneficiaries of lower development costs, although the interviewer raises affordability concerns about hiring such expertise. For in-house departments and corporate buyers, the claims concern organizing matter histories and supporting pricing changes. Legal-tech vendors and consultancies face easier entry, free open-source substitutes and changing prices for development or implementation work. The episode does not establish lawyer displacement numbers or claim that these tools independently provide legal advice to the public.
